author: Bill O Boyle
title: Local Korean War veteran Joseph Barna offers New Year's reflections - NewsBreak
text:
By Bill O Boyle [email protected] ,
11 minutes ago In this Times Leader file photo, Cpl. Joe Barna, 95, is seen at St. Ann’s RC Cemetery in Freeland, ahead of Flag Day in 2024. Submitted Photo, file FREELAND — Cpl. Joseph Barna, a U.S. Marine who fought in the Korean War in 1952, has again offered his heartfelt thoughts on the new year.
“Happy New Year,” he said. “If I had to make one resolution, here it is. If you were in a war and stood feet away from a bullet hitting a young Marine or shrapnel into a soldier, I know what my New Year’s resolution would be. I would trade my life for either of them. I have lived through enough years. Let them see their grandkids as I have seen and held mine in my arms. As I get older, I sometimes feel that I’m running out of tomorrows.”
Barna, 95, went on to say more — much more.
“Your life is what’s behind you,” he said. “It’s what is ahead of you. But it all lies within you. How have you lived your life? We know the tradition that says: ‘I’m going to make a New Year’s resolution.’”
He asks, was there something in the past year that you wish you had done differently?
“I have always believed what I was doing was the right thing to do,” he said. “If I was wrong, I was to blame — no one else. It all comes down to believing in yourself. Resolutions to me are a way of saying, I could have done something a little different, but now it’s too late.”
All his life, Barna said he learned the greatest things you can possess are strong friendships — friends that will help you make the right decisions in life.
“Never worry too much about what lies ahead of you,” Barna said. “What you have done to that point will get you through whatever comes your way. If you live with friendship, love, faith, hope, courage, and think of others, you don’t have to say wait till next year to do things differently.”
Barna then asks, “Are resolutions the hope of what may happen?”
His answer is from his heart.
“I believe when I was born, God left a message on the bed next to my mother,” he said. “The message read: ‘When this boy is growing up, teach him to think with his head, but act with his heart.’
“I spent two years in the Marines. There, you don’t think for yourself — others tell you right from wrong, when to sit and when to stand. When to run and when to walk. You may find yourself in combat where there are no times for resolutions. Each day you live, you had one supreme goal — to stay alive.”
Barna said many parents prayed that their sons would come home and live a long life.
“Other parents had to bury a young boy who never got to be a father, who never got to be a grandfather, and who never got to be an old man,” he said. “What would have been their last resolution?”
Barna then ended with this:
“You are the only one who can decide what kind of life you want to live. It’s only one day at a time. When I sat in a trench for many nights, I only asked God for one thing — to see the sunrise the next morning.
“There are many things one asks for, but never receives. Be who you are and what you are, and only you can decide. No one controls your life but you.
“Happy New Year.”
